Video Anomaly Detection:
Granularity, Resolution, and Scene Bias
Sara Abdulaziz<sup>1</sup> and Egor Bondarev<sup>1</sup>
Eindhoven University of Technology, 5612 AE Eindhoven, Netherlands
s.e.a.m.abdulaziz@tue.nl
GitHub Code
Abstract. Frame-level area under the ROC curve (AUC) is the dom-
inant evaluation metric for weakly supervised video anomaly detection
(WSVAD). Its standard form measures whether an anomalous frame out-
ranks a normal frame drawn from anywhere in the test set. We refer to
this comparison as pooled AUC, since it aggregates frame pairs across test
videos regardless of source. Pooled AUC therefore credits both event lo-
calization and diferences between video sources. We audit this protocol
on UCF-Crime [20] across recent state-of-the-art models spanning difer-
ent backbone families. Holding each model’s frame scores fixed, we read
them under three pairing granularities: global, per anomaly category,
and within each video, then repeat the same three-granularity readout
on zero-shot scores computed from the models’ internal representations.
We assess ranking reliability with a paired video bootstrap. Three find-
ings follow. First, pooled AUC does not reliably predict within-video
anomaly localization: models with similar pooled scores exhibit large
localization diferences and rank reversals under stricter granularities.
Second, at the benchmark’s test-split size, pooled AUC lacks the reso-
lution to support state-of-the-art margins reported in the field. Within
each backbone family, it resolves no comparison at those margins, while
within-video AUC resolves several over identical predictions. Learned
representations further reveal that within-video anomaly structure and
detector localization are decoupled. Third, on normal footage alone, ev-
ery model we examine separates videos by recording properties, such as
resolution and color encoding, indicating that scene sensitivity is shared
across the setting rather than specific to any architecture. We publicly re-
lease a granularity-aware protocol computable from existing predictions
and scene-factor annotations for UCF-Crime.

1 Introduction
Weakly supervised video anomaly detection (WSVAD) aims to localize anoma-
lous events in long videos while using only video-level labels during training [20,
21,23]. Progress on VAD benchmarks [20,25] is commonly summarized by a single
metric: frame-level anomaly prediction, evaluated by the ROC-AUC (area under
the true positive rate vs. false positive rate curve) pooled across all anomalous-
normal frame pairs in the test set. AUC is threshold independent and admits
a useful ranking interpretation statistically. However, its statistical consistency
concerns precision at a given sample size, and does not guarantee that the target
objective is being measured [8, 11, 19]. A consistent estimator may still be too
imprecise to rank at a finite sample n, or can be faithful but estimating the
wrong quantity.
A WSVAD model scores positively in an AUC comparison whenever an
anomalous frame receives a larger anomaly score than a normal frame, regard-
less of whether the ordering follows the event semantics, behavior, or the footage
source. This exposes two distinct failures, indistinguishable by the metric. First,
a high AUC may not imply genuine anomaly detection. As the credited compar-
isons are overwhelmingly cross-video, a model’s predictions can be rewarded by
AUC while learning to separate recordings rather than actual anomaly events.
At deployment, a detector must rank anomalous intervals above normal ones
from the same camera stream. Thus, a model relying on cross-video separation
might produce constantly elevated scores, permanent false alarm, on anomaly-
associated cameras while missing anomalies in atypical contexts. Pooled AUC
cannot distinguish such failure from true localization. Second, the cross-video
evaluation protocol yields an AUC measure too coarse to support model ranking
reliably. As the easy cross-video pairs dominate the pool, they compress most
models AUC toward a common narrow range, which may fall within the metric’s
own sampling error [4, 7].
In this work, we investigate the evaluation process of WSVAD models. Us-
ing the same frame-level predictions produced by existing methods, we ask: (i)
what does the standard pooled evaluation actually measure, and does it resolve
models ranking reliably? (ii) Does the anomaly signal dominate in each model’s
learned representation, and to what extent do the final anomaly scores depend
on it? (iii) What determines anomaly score responses in entirely normal video
segments? (iv) Does the pooled AUC ranking hold when comparisons are re-
stricted to frames from the same recording? To answer these questions, we make
the following contributions:
A multi-granularity evaluation framework that reads the same predictions
under diferent pairing rules, disentangling cross-recording based separation
from within-video anomaly localization. We apply this to both final scores
and training-free prototypes constructed from learned representations.
– A resolution analysis of WSVAD benchmarks: by resampling test videos,
we test which pairwise model comparisons are statistically distinguishable
at each granularity. We reveal that standard pooled AUC cannot separate
models at the sub-point margins the field reports, whereas within-video AUC
can.

2 Related Work
Weakly supervised video anomaly detection. Since the introduction of the large-
scale UCF-Crime benchmark [20], weakly supervised video anomaly detection
has evolved rapidly. Models have progressed from basic temporal instance se-
lection to increasingly sophisticated mechanisms, including robust normality
modeling, memory-augmented representations, and multimodal vision-language
alignments [1, 10, 14, 21–24]. Across all works, methods are still predominantly
ranked by pooled AUC on UCF-Crime, which is the protocol under question in
this study. Rather than proposing a new VAD model, we examine whether this
evaluation protocol supports the temporal-localization conclusions drawn from
the same models and predictions.
Evaluation protocols for video anomaly detection. Limitations of frame-level ag-
gregation have previously been identified from several complementary perspec-
tives. Ramachandra and Jones [15] introduced region-based and track-based de-
tection criteria because frame-level AUC rewards a video frame whenever any
score exceeds the threshold, without establishing that the anomalous object
or trajectory was correctly localized. Their analysis exposes a spatial credit-
assignment problem, where the rank statistic may be computed correctly while
the set of credited detections does not correspond to the intended task. Liu et
al. [9] identify three limitations of current VAD evaluation, which are the reliance
on a single-perspective temporal annotations, failure to reward early anomaly
detection, and the inability of existing benchmarks to reveal scene overfitting.
They address these limitations with annotation-averaged AUC/AP, Latency-
aware Average Precision (LaAP), and hard-normal benchmarks constructed to
test whether models generalize beyond anomaly-associated scenes. Rashvand et
al. [16] focus on the limitation of frame-level evaluation, where it treats a video
as a collection of isolated frames, while an anomaly is a coherent temporal event
with an onset and duration. The authors introduce an event-centric protocol
based on temporal-IoU event matching and multi-threshold event-level

5 Experimental Results
5.1 Dataset and Implementation Details
The headline analysis in this work emphasizes comparisons across recent top-
tier WSVAD methods with diferent backbone families. Table 1 presents the
models examined in this work. We adopt the oficial UCF-Crime [20] dataset for
the three-granularity evaluation and scene-reliance analysis. We use the frame-
level temporal annotations provided by [2]. For feature extraction, we adopt
the same public I3D, VideoMAEv2, and CLIP features produced in previous
works [2, 3, 10, 21, 23, 24]. Snippet size is set to 16 in all experiments. For CLIP-
based variants, we substitute the center frame feature for the snippet. Global,
per-category, and within-video scores are computed from the public pre-trained
checkpoint predictions, except for few models remarked in Table 1, which we
re-train. Prototype-based AUC refers to the AUC computed on probe features
extracted from the frozen VAD models. Score-based AUC is calculated from the
prediction scores of the VAD models based on the oficial ground truths, whereas
Prob-AUC is computed on soft multi-annotator labels [9]. All AUC values are
reported on the oficial UCF-Crime test set (290 video). The scene-factor audit
in Section 4 has a larger support, including all videos from the train and test
sets, to provide adequate scene diversity. The audit is descriptive rather than
a performance estimate. No model is trained, selected, or calibrated on these
annotations.
5.2 Anomaly Signal in Learned Representations
Table 2 (left-most column group) reports prototype-based AUC at the three
granularities, computed without the model’s classification head. At the video
granularity, the anomaly direction is built per video, leaving the query snippet
out when constructing the normal and abnormal prototypes. Since ground truth
frame labels are used to construct the prototypes, we treat AUC as a diagnostic
ceiling on accessible signal, not as achievable detection performance.
The frozen backbones already contain a dominant within-video anomaly rep-
resentation. VideoMAEv2 and I3D achieve a within-video ZS-AUC of 90.30 −
90.47, while CLIP reaches 88.34. Training WVAD models on these features does
not consistently strengthen this signal. Compared to VideoMAEv2, within-video
ZS-AUC decreases to 71.97 for UR-DMU, 74.11 for BN-WVAD, and 73.62 for
SST-WSVADL. This indicates that the learned representations substantially at-
tenuate the linearly accessible anomaly structure already present in the frozen
backbone. In contrast, CLIP-based models exhibit a diferent behavior, improv-
ing the oracle ZS-AUC over the frozen CLIP backbone. These models retain or
even strengthen a locally accessible anomaly direction, despite their lower global
ZS-AUC. This suggests that the observed behavior is not a universal conse-
quence of WSVAD training and therefore cannot yet be attributed to the choice
of backbone, temporal receptive field, or architectural design.

Storyline for Auditing Frame-Level AUC in Weakly Supervised
Video Anomaly Detection (WSVAD): Granularity, Resolution, and
Scene Bias
1. Why interesting?
a WSVAD temporally localizes the frames that belong to hazardous incidents or criminal behaviors
in long surveillance video.
b In practice, decisions are made on one camera stream: an anomalous frame’s score must outrank
the normal frames’ scores in that same stream.
c Standard benchmarks, such as UCF-Crime [8], provide only video-level binary labels (anoma-
ly/normal) over videos from diverse recordings and scenes; models trained on these labels must
localize at the frame-level.
d This encourages shortcuts: learning scene or recording properties that co-vary with anomalies
rather than the anomalies themselves.
e The evaluation protocol neither distinguishes nor flags this failure mode, yet it is still used to
report new state of the art.
2. How done now?
a Some work targets spatial (pixel-level) localization rather than temporal detection, but frame-
level spatial annotations are scarce.
b Other work shifts to VLM-based models that detect anomalies from contextual descriptions; the
confounded protocol is still adopted, and does not separate these methods or establish significance
in their reported AUC.
c Refinements of the protocol report additional metrics alongside the main one.
3. What is missing, and So What?
a Refining the protocol helps, but most reported metrics share the same problem.
b The standard metric is pooled AUC: ROC-AUC computed over all frame-level predictions pooled
across test videos; it reflects only a model’s ranking ability.
c In a pooled comparison, the two frames of a pair come from diferent recordings, so pooled AUC
(and any metric built on the same pairs) can be satisfied by separating recordings, not localizing
events. We argue that the confound lives in the pairing, not the scoring.
4. Proposed approach (P).
a Hold scores fixed; change the pairing (which frames are compared), not how they are scoring.
b Read the same scores at three granularities: global, per-category, within-video (same recording).
c Probe the learned representation directly from pre-trained WSVAD models, to separate what the
representation encodes from what the trained head delivers.
d Test claimed gains as paired diferences on shared video resamples (video-level uncertainty).
e Audit scene reliance directly: score normal-only frames by recording or semantic factors.
5. Experimental questions.
a Does pooled AUC reward recording separation over within-video localization?
c1: same scores, three granularities, matched backbones.
c2: models rank normal-vs-anomalous well when pooled (≈85–90).
c3: within-video drops sharply; rankings reverse.
c4: learned representation probe ⊥ delivered localization (decoupled).
b Can the metric resolve the margins the field reports?
c1: paired diferences on shared video resamples, per backbone family.
c2/c3: 0 pairs resolved at 0.4–0.5 margins; within-video resolves several.
c4: refining the score (Prob-AUC, soft labels) leaves ranking unchanged.
c Does the scene confound occur in real data?

Auditing Frame-Level AUC in WSVAD
Storyline for Auditing Frame-Level AUC in Weakly Supervised
Video Anomaly Detection (WSVAD): Granularity, Resolution, and
Scene Bias
1. Why interesting?
a WSVAD temporally localizes the frames that belong to hazardous incidents or criminal behaviors
in long surveillance video.
b In practice, decisions are made on one camera stream: an anomalous frame’s score must outrank
the normal frames’ scores in that same stream.
c Standard benchmarks, such as UCF-Crime [8], provide only video-level binary labels (anoma-
ly/normal) over videos from diverse recordings and scenes; models trained on these labels must
localize at the frame-level.
d This encourages shortcuts: learning scene or recording properties that co-vary with anomalies
rather than the anomalies themselves.
e The evaluation protocol neither distinguishes nor flags this failure mode, yet it is still used to
report new state of the art.
2. How done now?
a Some work targets spatial (pixel-level) localization rather than temporal detection, but frame-
level spatial annotations are scarce.
b Other work shifts to VLM-based models that detect anomalies from contextual descriptions; the
confounded protocol is still adopted, and does not separate these methods or establish significance
in their reported AUC.
c Refinements of the protocol report additional metrics alongside the main one.
3. What is missing, and So What?
a Refining the protocol helps, but most reported metrics share the same problem.
b The standard metric is pooled AUC: ROC-AUC computed over all frame-level predictions pooled
across test videos; it reflects only a model’s ranking ability.
c In a pooled comparison, the two frames of a pair come from diferent recordings, so pooled AUC
(and any metric built on the same pairs) can be satisfied by separating recordings, not localizing
events. We argue that the confound lives in the pairing, not the scoring.
4. Proposed approach (P).
a Hold scores fixed; change the pairing (which frames are compared), not how they are scoring.
b Read the same scores at three granularities: global, per-category, within-video (same recording).
c Probe the learned representation directly from pre-trained WSVAD models, to separate what the
representation encodes from what the trained head delivers.
d Test claimed gains as paired diferences on shared video resamples (video-level uncertainty).
e Audit scene reliance directly: score normal-only frames by recording or semantic factors.
5. Experimental questions.
a Does pooled AUC reward recording separation over within-video localization?
c1: same scores, three granularities, matched backbones.
c2: models rank normal-vs-anomalous well when pooled (≈85–90).
c3: within-video drops sharply; rankings reverse.
c4: learned representation probe ⊥ delivered localization (decoupled).
b Can the metric resolve the margins the field reports?
c1: paired diferences on shared video resamples, per backbone family.
c2/c3: 0 pairs resolved at 0.4–0.5 margins; within-video resolves several.
c4: refining the score (Prob-AUC, soft labels) leaves ranking unchanged.
c Does the scene confound occur in real data?

at higher speeds for extra verification of the presence of a scene factor. A video
is assigned a label only when the criterion holds for the majority of its duration;
borderline or mixed cases are marked ambiguous and dropped from that factor.

included for others. Ambiguity was mostly present in factors, such as camera
elevation, field of view, and concurrent activities.

S1.3 Bias-AUC under unequal pole sizes
The scene-factor supports in Section 4 are often imbalanced, as shown in Figure 3
and Table S1. For instance, 757 colored videos vs. 142 grayscale videos. This
raises a concern: could a reported bias-AUC far from 0.5 merely reflect this
imbalance rather than a genuine scene response? We answer this briefly. bias-
AUC estimates a pairwise ranking probability rather than a proportion. Thus, it
is invariant to how many videos fall at each pole [4]. A model that ranks videos
neutrally with respect to the factor obtains bias-AUC of 0.5 regardless of pole
sizes, rather than drifting toward the majority prevalence. Imbalance instead
widens the video-bootstrap interval (fewer videos in the minority pole give a
noisier estimate) without shifting its expected value.
